grammar.explanation:
~기도 하다 adds 'also' or 'sometimes' to a whole action or description. Use it when something is true on top of what you would expect, or when it happens now and then rather than always. 영화를 봐요 just says 'I watch movies'. 영화를 보기도 해요 says 'I also watch movies' or 'I sometimes watch movies'.

To form it, turn the stem into a noun with ~기 (Lesson 29), add the particle ~도 ('also'), then add 하다. 보다 → 보 + 기 → 보기 + 도 → 보기도 해요. 읽다 → 읽기도 해요. Vowel or consonant ending makes no difference. Adjectives work the same way: 밉다 → 밉기도 해요 'is sometimes annoying, too'.

Tense and politeness go only on the final 하다: 보기도 했어요 'also watched', 보기도 할 거예요 'will also watch'. A common mistake is putting the tense inside: 봤기도 해요 is wrong.

Compare ~도 on a noun: 영화도 봐요 means 'I watch movies too' (movies as well as other things). 영화를 보기도 해요 puts the 'also' on the whole action.

examples.ko: 저는 가끔 혼자 영화를 보기도 해요.
examples.en: I sometimes watch movies alone, too.
Sometimes tears come out when you cut onions.
That person also teaches chemistry.
I sometimes boil milk in the morning.
That person is sometimes annoying, too.
examples.note: Adjectives take ~기도 하다 the same way: 밉 + 기도 해요.

examples.en: Yesterday I also apologized to my friend.
examples.note: Only the final 하다 shows the past: 사과하기도 했어요.

examples.en: Do you also exercise on weekends?

grammar.explanation:
Use this pattern when two things are both true about the same situation: 'A, and also B' or 'both A and B'. It is common for mixed feelings (a movie that was both sad and fun) and for a range of activities you do at different times. The two parts can even be opposites.

Form: stem A + 기도 하고, then stem B + 기도 하다. Only the last 하다 changes for tense and politeness. 읽다, 만나다 → 읽기도 하고 만나기도 해요. Past: 슬프다, 재미있다 → 슬프기도 하고 재미있기도 했어요 (not 슬펐기도 하고).

Compare plain ~고 (Lesson 17): 책을 읽고 친구를 만나요 just lists two actions and can suggest an order, first one and then the other. With ~기도 하고 ~기도 하다 there is no time order. The two things each happen sometimes, or they are two sides of the same thing.

examples.ko: 저는 주말에 책을 읽기도 하고 친구를 만나기도 해요.
examples.en: On weekends I read books and also meet friends.

examples.ko: 그 영화는 슬프기도 하고 재미있기도 했어요.
examples.en: That movie was both sad and fun.

examples.ko: 저는 대학교에서 철학을 공부하기도 하고 화학을 공부하기도 했어요.
examples.en: At university I studied both philosophy and chemistry.

examples.ko: 이 일은 쉽기도 하고 어렵기도 해요.
examples.en: This work is easy in some ways and hard in others.

examples.ko: 혼자 사는 것은 편하기도 하고 외롭기도 해요.
examples.en: Living alone is both comfortable and lonely.

examples.ko: 어제는 비가 오기도 하고 눈이 오기도 했어요.
examples.en: Yesterday it rained and also snowed.
examples.note: The tense sits only on the last 하다: 오기도 하고 … 오기도 했어요.

grammar.explanation:
Use this to report what someone said in your own words: 'he said that...'. The quote drops the speaker's 요 or 습니다. Instead, the quoted verb goes into the plain form used in writing, then ~고 links it to a reporting verb such as 하다 or 말하다. The reporting verb carries the real tense and politeness: 했어요 'said'.

Present tense, step by step. Stem ends in a vowel → add ㄴ다: 가다 → 간다 → 간다고 했어요. Stem ends in a consonant → add 는다: 먹다 → 먹는다 → 먹는다고 했어요. ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ and take ㄴ다: 살다 → 산다고. Negative 않다 acts like a verb: 먹지 않는다고.

Past tense: past stem + 다고. 하다 → 했 + 다고 → 했다고. 먹다 → 먹었다고. Future: ~(으)ㄹ 거라고 (갈 거라고, 먹을 거라고) or ~겠다고 (가겠다고).

The tense inside the quote is the tense of the original words. 친구가 간다고 했어요 means my friend said 'I'm going'.

examples.en: My friend said he is going to Korea tomorrow.
My younger sibling said they finished all their homework.

examples.ko: 그 소설가가 새 책을 쓸 거라고 했어요.
examples.en: The novelist said she will write a new book.
The kids said they are planting trees.
The novelist said she lives in Seoul.
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ: 살 + ㄴ다고 → 산다고.

examples.en: My younger sibling said they don't eat meat.
examples.note: 않다 follows the verb pattern here: 않 + 는다고.

grammar.explanation:
Adjectives are simpler than verbs. In the plain form, an adjective's present tense is just its dictionary form: 바쁘다, 피곤하다. So you add ~고 straight to it: 바쁘다 → 바쁘다고 했어요. Never add ㄴ/는 to an adjective: 바쁜다고 is wrong.

있다 and 없다, and words built on them like 재미있다 and 맛없다, also take just ~다고: 시간이 없다고 했어요.

Past tense uses 았/었 + 다고, as with verbs: 바쁘다 → 바빴다고. Irregulars change as usual: 춥다 → 추웠다고. For a negative, put 안 in front: 안 비싸다고.

As always, the reporting verb (하다, 말하다) at the end carries the final tense and politeness.

examples.en: Minsu said he is very tired today.
The teacher said this problem is difficult.
My friend said that room is tiny.
My friend said she doesn't have time today.

examples.ko: 친구가 어제 날씨가 너무 추웠다고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend said the weather was really cold yesterday.
examples.note: 춥다 is ㅂ irregular: 춥 → 추웠다고.

examples.ko: 언니가 그 식당이 안 비싸다고 했어요.
examples.en: My older sister said that restaurant isn't expensive.

grammar.explanation:
When the original sentence was 'X is Y' with 이다, the quote ends in ~(이)라고 instead of ~다고. Noun ends in a consonant → 이라고: 학생 → 학생이라고. Noun ends in a vowel → 라고: 의사 → 의사라고. A common mistake is 학생이다고, which is wrong.

The negative 아니다 becomes 아니라고. The noun before it keeps 이/가 as usual: 학생이 아니라고 했어요.

Past tense: consonant → 이었다고 (선생님이었다고), vowel → 였다고 (친구였다고).

This form is also how you give a name: 저는 김민수라고 합니다 'I'm called Kim Minsu'. Statements with nouns use ~(이)라고; later you will see questions use ~(이)냐고.

examples.en: That man said he is a doctor.
My friend said this is her bag.
That person said he is not a student.
My name is Kim Minsu.
Grandma said she was a teacher when she was young.
examples.note: Past after a consonant: 선생님 + 이었다고.

examples.ko: 민수가 그 사람이 자기 친구였다고 했어요.
examples.en: Minsu said that person was his friend.
examples.note: Past after a vowel: 친구 + 였다고.

grammar.point: Other verbs used with quotes (생각하다, 믿다, 약속하다, 부르다)
grammar.explanation:
A ~다고 or ~(이)라고 clause works like a 'that...' clause in English. So it can come before verbs of thinking and believing, not just saying. 생각하다: 재미있다고 생각해요 'I think (that) it's fun'. 믿다: 이길 거라고 믿어요 'I believe we'll win'. The quoted part follows the same rules as before: ㄴ/는다 for verbs, 다 for adjectives, (이)라고 for nouns.

약속하다 (promise) usually takes a future quote: 갚겠다고 약속했어요 'promised to pay back'. Here ~겠다 shows the speaker's firm will: 'I will do it'.

부르다 (call) pairs with a noun quote: A를 B(이)라고 부르다 'call A B'. 부르다 is irregular: 부르 + 어요 → 불러요.

To say you don't think something, negate 생각하다 or the quote: 어렵다고 생각하지 않아요 or 어렵지 않다고 생각해요.

examples.en: I think this movie is fun.

examples.ko: 저는 우리 팀이 이길 거라고 믿어요.
examples.en: I believe our team will win.
I promised to pay back the debt by tomorrow.
Koreans call this gimbap.
My friends call me a big eater.
examples.note: 부르다 is irregular: 부르 + 어요 → 불러요.

examples.ko: 저는 그 문제가 어렵지 않다고 생각해요.
examples.en: I think that problem isn't difficult.

grammar.explanation:
Two quick conversation uses of quotes. First, 뭐 'what' + 라고 asks what someone said: 뭐라고 했어요? 'What did he say?'. 뭐 ends in a vowel, so it takes 라고. On its own, 뭐라고요? is a polite 'Sorry, what did you say?'. Said sharply, it can sound like 'What did you just say?!', so mind your tone.

The same 뭐라고 asks what something is called: 이것을 한국어로 뭐라고 해요?

Second, you can repeat what you heard as a quote, add 요 and raise your tone to check it or show surprise: 시험이 있다고요? 'You said there's a test?'. The usual quote rules apply: verbs → ㄴ/는다고요 (그만둔다고요?), adjectives and 있다/없다 → 다고요 (있다고요?), nouns → (이)라고요 (의사라고요?).

examples.en: What did the teacher say?
What did you say?
You said there's a test tomorrow?
What is this called in Korean?
Minsu is quitting his job? Did I hear that right?
That person is a doctor? Really?

grammar.point: Quoted clause before a noun: ~ㄴ/는다는 것/사실/소문
grammar.explanation:
Sometimes you want to talk about a piece of news itself: 'the rumor that...', 'the fact that...'. Korean takes the quote ~다고 하는 ('that is said to...') and shortens it to ~다는 in front of the noun. Common nouns are 것, 사실 (fact), 소문 (rumor), 말 (words) and 이야기 (story).

Build the quote first, then change 다고 to 다는:
그만두다 → 그만둔다고 → 그만둔다는 소문
많다 → 많다고 → 많다는 사실
결혼했다 → 결혼했다고 → 결혼했다는 것
For nouns, (이)라고 becomes (이)라는: 의사라고 → 의사라는 사실.

Compare plain ~는 것 (Lesson 26): 회사를 그만두는 것 just describes the action. 회사를 그만둔다는 소문 marks it as information someone said or heard.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 회사를 그만둔다는 소문을 들었어요.
examples.en: I heard a rumor that he is quitting the company.
I didn't know that my friend has a lot of debt.
I found out yesterday that my sister got married.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 의사라는 사실을 아무도 몰랐어요.
examples.en: Nobody knew that he was a doctor.
examples.note: With 이다 the form is ~(이)라는: 의사 + 라는.

examples.en: I heard that it's going to rain tomorrow.

grammar.explanation:
Use this to report a suggestion: someone said 'let's...'. The original might have been 가자, 갑시다 or 가요 used as 'let's go'. In a quote, all of these become the plain ~자 (Lesson 44) + 고.

Form: stem + 자고. There is no vowel/consonant split: 가다 → 가자고, 먹다 → 먹자고, 만들다 → 만들자고. The reporting verb, usually 하다, carries tense and politeness.

For 'let's not', use stem + 지 말자고: 나가지 말자고 했어요.

Compare with statement quotes: 간다고 했어요 means 'he said he is going'. 가자고 했어요 means 'he suggested we go'.

examples.en: My friend suggested we watch a movie together.

examples.ko: 남자 친구가 주말에 바다에 가자고 했어요.
examples.en: My boyfriend suggested we go to the sea this weekend.
My younger sibling suggested we eat pizza for dinner.

examples.ko: 친구가 오늘은 밖에 나가지 말자고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend suggested we not go out today.
examples.note: 'Let's not' is ~지 말자고.

examples.en: My older sister suggested we take a photo together.
Who suggested going first?

grammar.explanation:
Use this to report a question someone asked: 'he asked if...' or 'she asked where...'. The reporting verb is usually 묻다 or 물어보다. 묻다 is ㄷ irregular: 묻 + 었어요 → 물었어요.

Form: verb stem + 냐고 (casual, most common in speech) or + 느냐고 (more formal, often written). There is no vowel/consonant split: 가다 → 가냐고, 먹다 → 먹냐고 (or 먹느냐고). ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ: 살다 → 사냐고. 있다 and 없다 work like verbs here: 있냐고, 없냐고.

Past: past stem + 냐고: 먹었냐고. Future: ~(으)ㄹ 거냐고: 할 거냐고.

Question words stay inside the quote: 어디에 가냐고, 뭘 먹냐고. Without a question word, translate it as 'asked if' or 'asked whether'.

examples.en: Mom asked me if I had eaten.
My friend asked me where I was going.
The doctor asked me if I smoke.
My friend asked me where I live.
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ: 살 + 냐고 → 사냐고.

examples.en: My younger sibling asked me if I had time.
examples.note: 묻다 is ㄷ irregular: 묻 → 물었어요.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 내일 뭘 할 거냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: My friend asked me what I'm going to do tomorrow.

grammar.explanation:
Adjectives follow the textbook pattern ~(으)냐고. Stem ends in a consonant → 으냐고: 넓다 → 넓으냐고, 좋다 → 좋으냐고. Stem ends in a vowel → 냐고: 바쁘다 → 바쁘냐고, 아프다 → 아프냐고.

In everyday speech most people drop the 으 and use 냐고 for every adjective: 넓냐고, 좋냐고. Both are understood. Words ending in 있다/없다 (맛있다, 재미없다) take 냐고: 맛있냐고.

Irregulars: ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ: 멀다 → 머냐고. ㅂ irregulars change before 으: 춥다 → 추우냐고 (casual 춥냐고).

Past tense is the same for every adjective: 았/었 + 냐고 → 바빴냐고, 어려웠냐고.

examples.en: My friend asked me if I'm busy these days.
That person asked if the room is big.
Mom asked if the food was tasty.
My friend asked me if the exam was hard.
My friend asked if school is far from home.
examples.note: 멀다 drops ㄹ: 멀 + 냐고 → 머냐고.

examples.en: The doctor asked where it hurts.

grammar.explanation:
For questions like 'Are you a student?' or 'What is this?', the 이다 at the end becomes ~(이)냐고 in the quote. Noun ends in a consonant → 이냐고: 학생 → 학생이냐고. Noun ends in a vowel → 냐고: 의사 → 의사냐고, 뭐 → 뭐냐고, 누구 → 누구냐고.

The negative 아니다 becomes 아니냐고: 학생이 아니냐고.

Past: consonant → 이었냐고, vowel → 였냐고: 누구였냐고.

Remember the noun family: statements use ~(이)라고, questions use ~(이)냐고.

examples.en: That person asked me if I was a student.
My friend asked what this was.
The teacher asked who that man was.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 그 사람이 남자 친구냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: My friend asked me if that guy was my boyfriend.

examples.ko: 엄마가 어제 만난 사람이 누구였냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: Mom asked who the person I met yesterday was.
examples.note: Past after a vowel: 누구 + 였냐고.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 저에게 한국 사람이 아니냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: That person asked me if I wasn't Korean.

grammar.explanation:
A direct quote repeats someone's exact words, like using quotation marks in English. Put the words in quotation marks, add 라고 (or 하고), then 하다 or 말하다: "안녕하세요"라고 했어요.

Nothing inside the quotation marks changes. The speech level, 요 and tense stay exactly as they were said. Compare the same words both ways: direct "배고파요"라고 했어요, indirect 배고프다고 했어요.

In a direct quote it is always 라고, even after a consonant: "감사합니다"라고. 하고 also works, and is common in speech.

examples.en: The child said, "I'm hungry."
The man said, "Hello."
Mom said, "Come quickly."
The gentleman said, "Thank you."
examples.note: Direct quotes always use 라고, even after a consonant.

examples.en: My friend asked, "Where are you going?"
The teacher said, "Do your homework by tomorrow."

grammar.explanation:
Use this to report an order or instruction: 'she told me to...'. The original might have been polite (드세요, 읽으세요) or casual (먹어, 읽어라). In a quote they all become ~(으)라고.

Form: stem ends in a vowel → 라고: 자다 → 자라고, 마시다 → 마시라고. Stem ends in a consonant → 으라고: 읽다 → 읽으라고. ㄹ stems take 라고 directly: 만들다 → 만들라고. ㄷ irregulars change: 듣다 → 들으라고.

The person told to do it takes ~에게 or ~한테. The command itself has no tense; the tense goes on the reporting verb: 했어요.

Don't mix up three similar quotes. 간다고 했어요 = said he is going (statement). 가자고 했어요 = suggested we go (suggestion). 가라고 했어요 = told me to go (command).

examples.en: The teacher told the students to read the book.
Mom told me to go to bed early.

examples.ko: 의사가 저에게 물을 많이 마시라고 했어요.
examples.en: The doctor told me to drink a lot of water.
The manager told me to attend the meeting.
Mom told me to make dinner.
examples.note: ㄹ stems keep the ㄹ and add 라고: 만들 + 라고.

examples.ko: 선생님이 원어민의 발음을 잘 들으라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher told us to listen carefully to native speakers' pronunciation.
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 → 들 + 으라고.

grammar.explanation:
Use this to report a negative command: 'he told me not to...'. The originals 가지 마세요, 가지 마 and 가지 마라 all become 가지 말라고 in a quote.

Form: stem + 지 (no vowel/consonant split), then 말라고. 말다 is an ㄹ stem, so it adds 라고 directly: 말 + 라고 → 말라고. 먹다 → 먹지 말라고, 가다 → 가지 말라고.

A common mistake is 안 가라고. Commands can't use 안, so 'told me not to go' is 가지 말라고 했어요.

Compare: 가지 말자고 했어요 = suggested we not go. 가지 말라고 했어요 = told me not to go.

examples.ko: 엄마가 저에게 늦게 오지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom told me not to come home late.

examples.ko: 선생님이 수업 시간에 떠들지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher told us not to chat during class.

examples.ko: 의사가 저에게 술을 마시지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: The doctor told me not to drink alcohol.

examples.ko: 아빠가 남에게 함부로 말하지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: Dad told me not to speak rudely to others.
The teacher told me not to worry.

examples.ko: 의사가 저에게 매운 음식을 먹지 말라고 했어요.
examples.en: The doctor told me not to eat spicy food.

grammar.point: Quoted requests for oneself: ~(아/어) 달라고 하다
grammar.explanation:
When someone asks for something to be given to them, Korean reports it with 달다, not 주다. Original 물 주세요 → quote 물을 달라고 했어요. 달다 only appears in quotes like this, never on its own.

The same happens with ~아/어 주다 'do something for me': 빌려 주세요 → 빌려 달라고. Step by step: verb + 아/어, then 달라고. 닫다 → 닫아 달라고. 읽다 → 읽어 달라고. 하다 → 해 달라고. 묶다 → 묶어 달라고.

What matters is who benefits in the original sentence. If the original speaker asked for something for themselves, use 달라고, no matter who reports it later.

To report 'please don't...', use ~지 말아 달라고: 늦지 말아 달라고 했어요.

examples.en: My younger sibling asked me to give them water.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 돈을 빌려 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend asked me to lend him money.

examples.ko: 아이가 엄마에게 책을 읽어 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: The child asked mom to read him a book.
The customer asked us to close the window.

examples.ko: 동생이 저에게 신발 끈을 묶어 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling asked me to tie their shoelaces.
Grandma asked me to call her.
examples.note: 하다 contracts: 하 + 여 → 해 달라고.

grammar.point: Giving to someone else: 주라고 하다
grammar.explanation:
달라고 is only for 'give it to me', the original speaker. If the speaker told you to give something to someone else, use the normal command quote of 주다: 주 + 라고 → 주라고.

Compare. Mom says '동생한테 과자 줘' → 엄마가 동생한테 과자를 주라고 했어요. Mom says '나한테 과자 줘' → 엄마가 과자를 달라고 했어요.

The same choice applies to ~아/어 주다. 도와 달라고 = asked me to help them. 도와주라고 = told me to help someone else.

Tip: look at who gets the item or the help. The original speaker → 달라고. Anyone else → 주라고.

examples.ko: 엄마가 저에게 동생한테 과자를 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom told me to give my younger sibling some snacks.

examples.ko: 선생님이 저에게 이 책을 민수에게 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher told me to give this book to Minsu.

examples.ko: 친구가 저에게 그 편지를 여자 친구에게 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend told me to give that letter to his girlfriend.
The teacher told me to help Minsu.
examples.note: Minsu, not the teacher, gets the help, so it's 주라고.

examples.ko: 엄마가 저에게 강아지한테 물을 주라고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom told me to give the dog some water.
Who did they tell you to give this money to?

grammar.explanation:
부탁 is a noun meaning a favor or a request. 부탁이 있어요 = I have a favor to ask. 부탁을 들어 주다 = to do someone a favor (literally, to listen to their request).

부탁하다 is the verb 'to ask a favor'. The person you ask takes ~에게 or ~한테. What you ask for is often a quoted request: 도와 달라고 부탁했어요 = asked them to help me. It can also be a simple noun: 친구에게 강아지를 부탁했어요 = asked a friend to look after the dog.

Set phrases you will hear a lot: 부탁해요 'I'm counting on you / please', and 잘 부탁드립니다 when you meet someone you'll work with.

Compare: 물어보다 asks for information. 부탁하다 asks for help or an action.

examples.en: I have a favor to ask.
I asked my friend to help me move.

examples.ko: 제 부탁을 들어 줄 수 있어요?
examples.en: Can you do me a favor?
I asked my friend to look after my dog during my trip.

examples.ko: 동생에게 제 방에 들어오지 말아 달라고 부탁했어요.
examples.en: I asked my younger sibling not to come into my room.
examples.note: 'Please don't' in a quote is ~지 말아 달라고.

examples.en: Please do me just one favor.

lessons.title: Lesson 56: To make, to let: ~게 하다, ~게: so that

grammar.point: To make / let someone do: ~게 하다
grammar.explanation:
~게 하다 means 'make someone do', 'let someone do', or 'make something a certain way'. Korean uses the same form for forcing and allowing, so context decides the English.

Form: stem + 게 하다, with no vowel/consonant split. Only 하다 changes for tense. 자다 → 자게 했어요. 먹다 → 먹게 해요. Adjectives describe the state you cause: 기쁘다 → 기쁘게 했어요 'made happy'.

The person made to act is usually marked with ~을/를 (저를 자게 했어요) or ~에게 (아이에게 채소를 먹게 해요). If the inside clause already has an object, the person often takes ~이/가: 동생이 게임을 못 하게 했어요.

'Not let / stop someone' is 못 ~게 하다 or ~지 못하게 하다: 못 가게 했어요. ~지 않게 하다 means 'make sure something doesn't happen'.

examples.en: Mom made me go to bed early.
The teacher let the students go home.
That news surprised me.

examples.ko: 아빠가 동생이 게임을 못 하게 했어요.
examples.en: Dad didn't let my younger sibling play games.
My friend's letter made me happy.
examples.note: With an adjective, ~게 하다 means 'make (someone) feel that way'.

examples.ko: 부모님이 아이에게 매일 채소를 먹게 해요.
examples.en: The parents make their child eat vegetables every day.

grammar.point: So that / in a way that: ~게 + verb
grammar.explanation:
Here ~게 is followed by an ordinary verb, not 하다, and means 'so that...' or 'in a way that...'. The ~게 clause comes first and gives the goal. The main verb says what you do to reach it.

Form: stem + 게, with no vowel/consonant split: 보다 → 보게, 먹다 → 먹게. Two very common combinations:
~(으)ㄹ 수 있게 'so that someone can': 볼 수 있게, 들을 수 있게.
~지 않게 'so that something doesn't happen': 늦지 않게, 걸리지 않게.

Tense goes only on the final verb: 늦지 않게 일찍 출발했어요 (not 늦지 않았게).

This is the same ~게 that turns adjectives into adverbs: 크다 → 크게, 따뜻하다 → 따뜻하게. Compare ~(으)려고 (Lesson 32), which is about the subject's own intention. ~게 often aims at a result for someone else or for the situation.

examples.ko: 아이들이 잘 볼 수 있게 글씨를 크게 써 주세요.
examples.en: Please write big so the kids can see well.

examples.ko: 다른 사람들이 들을 수 있게 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so others can hear.
Leave early so you are not late.
I closed the window so the rain wouldn't come in.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸리지 않게 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.
examples.en: Dress warmly so you don't catch a cold.

examples.ko: 동생이 잘 수 있게 텔레비전을 껐어요.
examples.en: I turned off the TV so my younger sibling could sleep.
examples.note: 끄다 drops ㅡ: 끄 + 었어요 → 껐어요.

grammar.explanation:
Many 하다 verbs are a noun + 하다: 공부하다, 화해하다, 소개하다. Replace 하다 with 시키다 and the meaning becomes 'make or get someone to do it': 공부하다 'to study' → 공부시키다 'to make someone study'.

The person made to act takes ~을/를: 동생을 공부시켜요. Conjugate 시키다 like any verb: 시키 + 어요 → 시켜요, past 시켰어요.

With feeling verbs it means 'cause the feeling': 실망하다 'be disappointed' → 실망시키다 'disappoint someone'. 흥분하다 → 흥분시키다 'get someone excited'.

It means roughly the same as ~하게 하다 (Lesson 56): 공부시켜요 = 공부하게 해요. Not every 하다 verb can take 시키다, so learn the common ones. 소개시키다 is very common in speech, but 소개하다 is considered more standard.

examples.en: Mom makes my younger sibling study every day.
I got my two friends to make up.
That news disappointed my parents.
My parents enrolled me in that school.
examples.note: 입학하다 (to start at a school) → 입학시키다 (to enrol someone).

examples.en: Who got the kids all excited?
My friend reminded me of the appointment.
examples.note: 상기시키다 is only used in its 시키다 form: A에게 B를 상기시키다.

grammar.point: 시키다 as a verb: to order
grammar.explanation:
On its own, 시키다 has two everyday meanings. At restaurants or for delivery it means 'to order' food or drinks: 피자를 시켰어요. This is the usual word in conversation; 주문하다 is more formal.

It also means 'to order someone to do a task': person + 에게, task + 을/를, then 시키다. Typical tasks are 일 (work), 심부름 (an errand) and 청소 (cleaning). 엄마가 저에게 청소를 시켰어요 = Mom had me clean.

Conjugation: 시키 + 어요 → 시켜요. Past 시켰어요. 'Shall we order?' 시킬까요?

examples.en: We ordered pizza.
Mom sent me on an errand.
My manager gives me a lot of work.
What shall we order?
I ordered two cups of coffee.
The teacher had the students clean up.

grammar.explanation:
~(이)나 joins two nouns as choices: 'A or B'. Use it when either option is fine. Noun ends in a consonant → 이나: 빵 → 빵이나. Noun ends in a vowel → 나: 커피 → 커피나.

Only the first noun takes ~(이)나. The second takes whatever particle the sentence needs: 빵이나 밥을 먹어요 (object), 엄마나 아빠가 와요 (subject). Shared particles like ~에서, ~에 and ~(으)로 usually appear only after the last noun: 버스나 택시로, 체육관이나 공원에서.

Don't confuse it with 'and'. ~하고 and ~와/과 mean both. ~(이)나 means one or the other.

examples.en: I will eat bread or rice.

examples.ko: 엄마나 아빠가 저를 학교에 데려다 줄 거예요.
examples.en: Mom or dad will take me to school.
Shall I get you coffee or tea?
I'll go by bus or taxi.
I exercise at the gym or in the park.
examples.note: ~에서 comes only once, after the last noun.

examples.en: Do you have time on the weekend or after school?

grammar.point: Settling for something: ~(이)나 with one option
grammar.explanation:
With only one noun, ~(이)나 changes meaning. It shows you are settling for something: it's not ideal, but it will do. English often uses 'just' or '... or something': 텔레비전이나 봐요 = Let's just watch TV.

The form is the same: consonant → 이나 (잠 → 잠이나), vowel → 나 (영화 → 영화나). It replaces 을/를 or 이/가.

It's common in suggestions and plans: ~(이)나 + ~(으)ㄹ까요?, ~아/어야겠어요, or ~(으)ㄹ 거예요.

Because it implies 'nothing better', be careful when offering something to a guest. 커피 드릴까요? is better than 커피나 드릴까요?, which can sound like 'want coffee or whatever?'.

examples.en: On weekends I just watch TV at home.
Shall we just have ramen for lunch?
I'm tired, so I guess I'll just sleep at home.
Shall we just watch a movie this weekend?
examples.note: 영화 ends in a vowel, so it takes 나.

examples.ko: 비가 오면 집에서 책이나 읽을 거예요.
examples.en: If it rains, I'll just read a book at home.
If you're tired, just have a coffee.

grammar.explanation:
~거나 joins two actions or descriptions as choices: 'do A or do B', 'is A or B'. It is the verb and adjective version of ~(이)나.

Form: stem + 거나, with no vowel/consonant split: 읽다 → 읽거나, 쓰다 → 쓰거나, 피곤하다 → 피곤하거나. Only the last verb shows tense and politeness: 운동하거나 친구들과 놀았어요 = exercised or hung out with friends.

You can also say A거나 B거나 하다: 책을 읽거나 운동을 하거나 해요.

Don't mix them up. Nouns use ~(이)나: 책이나 신문. Verbs and adjectives use ~거나: 책을 읽거나 신문을 봐요.

examples.en: On weekends I read or exercise.
I'll write my friend a letter or call him.
If you're tired or sick, rest at home.
In the evening I listen to music or take a walk.

examples.ko: 학생 때는 방과후에 체육관에서 운동하거나 친구들과 놀았어요.
examples.en: When I was a student, I worked out at the gym or hung out with friends after school.
examples.note: The past tense goes only on the last verb: 놀았어요.

examples.ko: 모르는 단어가 있으면 사전을 찾거나 선생님께 물어보세요.
examples.en: If there's a word you don't know, look it up in a dictionary or ask the teacher.
